title: Subject-Verb Agreement
summary: How to locate the real subject of a verb and choose singular or plural when the noun beside the verb is misleading.

sections.heading: Find the head of the subject
sections.body:
The verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, not with the nearest noun. Material that comes between them — a prepositional phrase, a relative clause, an appositive, a phrase in commas — never changes the agreement.

The reliable test is to delete everything between the head and the verb and read what is left. `The list of approved items is updated` reduces to `the list is`, so the plural `items` sitting next to the verb is irrelevant. The trap is strongest with `of` phrases, because the second noun is often the one carrying the meaning.

examples.right: The list of approved suppliers is updated every quarter.
examples.wrong: The list of approved suppliers are updated every quarter.
examples.note: The head is `list`, singular; `suppliers` belongs to the of-phrase.

examples.right: The impact of rising sea levels on coastal cities has been underestimated.
examples.wrong: The impact of rising sea levels on coastal cities have been underestimated.
examples.note: Two intervening plurals do not make the singular head plural.

examples.right: The professor, together with her two assistants, is attending the conference.
examples.wrong: The professor, together with her two assistants, are attending the conference.
examples.note: A phrase in commas adds information but not a second subject.

sections.heading: Quantifier + of + noun: the second noun decides
sections.body:
With the quantifiers **most, some, all, half, none, any, a lot of, the rest of** and with **percentages and fractions**, the pattern reverses: agreement follows the noun after `of`, because these words take their number from what they measure.

`Most of the water is polluted` but `Most of the students are satisfied`; `Half of the budget has been spent` but `Half of the grants have been withdrawn`; `Forty per cent of the sample was female` but `Forty per cent of the respondents were female`. `None of` is treated as singular in formal writing, though a plural verb is widely accepted.

examples.right: Most of the water in the reservoir has evaporated during the heatwave.
examples.wrong: Most of the water in the reservoir have evaporated.
examples.note: `Water` is uncountable, so the verb is singular.

examples.right: Most of the students who sat the exam were satisfied with the result.
examples.wrong: Most of the students who sat the exam was satisfied.
examples.note: The same quantifier, now measuring a plural noun.

examples.right: Two thirds of the funding comes from private donors.
examples.wrong: Two thirds of the funding come from private donors.
examples.note: Fractions and percentages agree with the noun they quantify.

sections.heading: Each, every, either, neither, one of
sections.body:
These are singular however plural the phrase around them looks. `Each of the proposals has merit`, `Every one of the samples was contaminated`, `Neither of the candidates meets the criteria`, `One of the machines has broken down`.

`One of the` is the commonest failure point, because the plural noun stands directly before the verb: the subject is `one`, not `machines`. Note the different structure in `one of the students who have applied`, where the relative clause describes `students` and correctly takes a plural verb.

When `each` follows a plural subject rather than heading it, the verb stays plural: `The proposals each have merit`.

examples.right: One of the machines has broken down again.
examples.wrong: One of the machines have broken down again.
examples.note: The head is `one`; `of the machines` only says which one.

examples.right: Neither of the two solutions addresses the underlying cause.
examples.wrong: Neither of the two solutions address the underlying cause.

examples.right: Every student and every member of staff was issued with a card.
examples.wrong: Every student and every member of staff were issued with a card.
examples.note: `Every` keeps the verb singular even across `and`.

sections.heading: A number of, the number of, and there is / there are
sections.body:
The pair **a number of** and **the number of** points in opposite directions. `A number of` means *several* and takes a plural verb: `A number of students have complained`. `The number of` names a figure, which is one thing, and takes a singular verb: `The number of complaints has risen`.

In **there** sentences the verb agrees with what follows it, not with `there`: `There is one exception` / `There are several exceptions`. With a compound subject, the verb conventionally agrees with the **nearer** noun, so word order decides: `There are two printers and a laptop in the office`, but `There is a laptop and two printers in the office`.

examples.right: A number of students have complained about the new timetable.
examples.wrong: A number of students has complained about the new timetable.
examples.note: `A number of` is a plural quantifier meaning several.

examples.right: The number of applications has risen sharply since the fee was scrapped.
examples.wrong: The number of applications have risen sharply.
examples.note: The subject is the figure itself, which is singular.

examples.right: There are two laboratories and a workshop on the ground floor.
examples.wrong: There is two laboratories and a workshop on the ground floor.
examples.note: The verb matches the nearer noun, here the plural `laboratories`.

sections.heading: And, or, nor, as well as, along with
sections.body:
Subjects joined by **and** are plural: `The report and the appendix were circulated`. The exception is a pair that names a single thing or is preceded by `each`/`every`: `Research and development is expensive`.

Subjects joined by **or** or **nor** take a verb agreeing with the **nearer** subject: `Neither the tutors nor the director was informed`; `Neither the director nor the tutors were informed`. Reversing the order changes the verb.

Phrases such as **as well as, along with, together with, in addition to, including** are not conjunctions. They add information to the subject without enlarging it, so the verb keeps the number of the original subject.

examples.right: The final report and the technical appendix were circulated on Monday.
examples.note: Two subjects joined by `and` are plural.

examples.right: Neither the supervisors nor the head of school was informed of the change.
examples.wrong: Neither the supervisors nor the head of school were informed.
examples.note: With `nor`, the verb follows the nearer subject, here singular `head`.

examples.right: The director, as well as several senior staff, is expected to attend.
examples.wrong: The director, as well as several senior staff, are expected to attend.
examples.note: `As well as` is not `and`; the subject is still `the director`.

sections.heading: Collectives, plural-looking nouns, clauses and gerunds
sections.body:
**Collective nouns** such as team, government, committee, staff, family and company take a singular verb in American English. British English allows both, choosing the plural when the members act individually (`the committee are divided`) and the singular when the body acts as a unit (`the committee has issued its report`). What matters is consistency: do not follow a plural verb with `its`, or a singular verb with `their`.

Some nouns look plural but are singular: `news`, `economics`, `mathematics`, `politics`, `physics`, `statistics` as a discipline, and diseases such as `measles`. `Statistics show a decline` is a different word, the plural of the countable `statistic`.

A **clause or gerund phrase** used as a subject is a single idea and takes a singular verb: `Reading academic papers in a second language is demanding`, `What the results show is worrying`, `Whether the trend continues remains unclear`.

examples.right: The committee publishes its report on Friday.
examples.wrong: The committee publish its report on Friday.
examples.note: A singular verb must be matched by singular `its`.

examples.right: Economics is often described as a social science.
examples.wrong: Economics are often described as a social science.
examples.note: The -s of the discipline name is not a plural.

examples.right: Reading academic papers in a second language requires considerable stamina.
examples.wrong: Reading academic papers in a second language require considerable stamina.
examples.note: A gerund subject counts as one thing, however long the phrase.

slips: Agreeing with the noun nearest the verb: `The list of items are`. Delete the of-phrase and the head noun becomes visible.
Making `one of the` plural: `One of the machines have broken down` should be `has`.
Confusing `a number of` (plural) with `the number of` (singular).
Treating `as well as`, `along with` and `together with` as if they were `and`. They leave the subject's number unchanged.
Putting a plural verb after `economics`, `politics`, `mathematics` or `news`, which are all singular.
Mixing a singular verb with `their`, or a plural verb with `its`, after a collective noun such as `team` or `government`.

questions.prompt: The list of approved suppliers ___ updated at the end of every quarter.
questions.explain: The head of the subject is `list`, not `suppliers`; the of-phrase between the two never changes the agreement.

questions.prompt: Most of the water in the reservoir ___ evaporated during the heatwave.
questions.explain: After `most of`, the noun following `of` decides. `Water` is uncountable and therefore singular, unlike `most of the students, who have...`.

questions.prompt: A number of students ___ complained about the way the timetable was changed.
questions.explain: `A number of` simply means several and takes a plural verb. `The number of students has risen` is the opposite pattern, where the figure is the subject.

questions.prompt: The committee ___ its final report on Friday morning.
questions.explain: The possessive `its` treats the committee as a single body, so the verb must be singular too; a plural verb would require `their`.

questions.prompt: Economics ___ often described as the most quantitative of the social sciences.
questions.explain: Discipline names ending in -s — economics, mathematics, politics, physics — are singular despite their form.

questions.prompt: Neither of the two proposed solutions ___ the underlying cause of the shortage.
questions.explain: `Neither` is the singular head of the subject; `of the two proposed solutions` only identifies the set it is chosen from.

questions.prompt: There ___ two printers and a laptop in the shared office.
questions.explain: In `there` sentences the verb agrees with what follows, and with a compound subject it takes the number of the nearer noun, here plural `printers`.

questions.prompt: Reading academic papers in a second language ___ considerable stamina and concentration.
questions.explain: A gerund phrase is a single subject however many plural nouns it contains, so the verb is singular.

questions.prompt: The number of applications for the scholarship ___ risen sharply since the fee was scrapped.
questions.explain: `The number of` names one figure and is singular; only `a number of`, meaning several, takes a plural verb.

questions.prompt: Forty per cent of the respondents ___ under the age of thirty.
questions.explain: A percentage takes its number from the noun after `of`; `respondents` is plural, whereas `forty per cent of the sample is` would be singular.

questions.prompt: The project leader, as well as her two research assistants, ___ attending the conference in Vienna.
questions.explain: `As well as` adds information without creating a compound subject, so the verb still agrees with the singular `project leader`.

questions.prompt: One of the machines in the testing lab ___ broken down again.
questions.explain: The subject is `one`; the plural `machines` sits inside the of-phrase and never governs the verb.
